questions.question: For an infinite set $X$, which bijection condition is equivalent to countable infinitude?
options: there is a bijection between $X$ and $\mathbb{N}$
there is a bijection between $X$ and $\mathbb{R}$
there is an injection from $\mathbb{N}$ into $X$
there is a bijection between $X$ and some $\{1,\dots,n\}$

questions.question: Which condition makes an infinite set uncountable?
options: no bijection between it and $\mathbb{N}$ exists
it has finitely many elements
it can be listed as a sequence
some of its elements lie outside $\mathbb{N}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$

questions.question: Which of these sets is countable?
options: $\mathbb{Q}$
$\mathbb{R}$
$\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$
the set of all intervals in $\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: Which of these sets is uncountable?
options: $\mathbb{R}$
$\mathbb{Q}$
$\mathbb{N}$

questions.question: Under the countable/uncountable classification, which possibilities exist for an infinite set?
options: either countable or uncountable
always countably infinite, like $\mathbb{N}$
uncountable unless it is a subset of $\mathbb{N}$
countable, uncountable, or neither

questions.question: What does it mean, intuitively, that a set is countably infinite?
options: Its elements can be listed in a sequence.
It has only finitely many elements.
Its elements fill a whole interval of the real line.
Its elements are all natural numbers.

questions.question: Is $\mathbb{N}$ countable?
options: Yes, the identity map is a bijection $\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$
No, because only finite sets are countable
Yes, because every subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is countable
Yes, because every infinite set is countable

questions.question: What does the subset result say about a subset $A$ of a countable set?
options: $A$ is countable
$A$ is necessarily uncountable
$A$ must equal $\mathbb{N}$
$A$ must be infinite

questions.question: If $A\subseteq\mathbb{Q}$ is infinite, what follows?
options: $A$ is countable
$A$ is uncountable
$A=\mathbb{R}$
$A$ must be all of $\mathbb{Q}$

questions.question: Why is it wrong to say every infinite set is countable?
options: $\mathbb{R}$ is infinite but uncountable
every infinite set is actually finite
$\mathbb{N}$ has no bijection with itself
$\mathbb{Q}$ is uncountable

questions.question: How do uncountable sets compare in size with countable sets?
options: They are strictly larger than countable sets
They are the same size, since both are infinite
They match $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, which is larger than $\mathbb{N}$
They are larger only when they are unbounded

questions.question: $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$. Does that make $\mathbb{Q}$ uncountable?
options: No: $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable despite being dense
Yes, density forces uncountability
No, but only because $\mathbb{Q}$ is a subset of $\mathbb{R}$
Yes: $\mathbb{Q}$ cannot be listed in increasing order

questions.question: To prove an infinite set $X$ is countable, what is enough?
options: Exhibiting one bijection between $X$ and $\mathbb{N}$
Showing one attempted bijection fails
Listing infinitely many distinct elements of $X$
Exhibiting a surjection from $X$ onto $\mathbb{N}$

questions.question: Is $\mathbb{Z}$ countable?
options: Yes; $\mathbb{Z}\subseteq\mathbb{Q}$ and is infinite
No, because $\mathbb{Z}$ includes negative numbers.
No, because $\mathbb{Z}$ is infinite
Only if $\mathbb{Z}$ is made finite

questions.question: Can a subset of an uncountable set be countable?
options: Yes: $\mathbb{N}\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ is countable while $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
No, subsets of uncountable sets are always uncountable
No, because subsets are always smaller and hence finite
Only if the subset equals the whole set

questions.question: Under the Math II convention, what must be established to prove a set $X$ is uncountable?
options: $X$ is infinite and no bijection $X\to\mathbb{N}$ exists.
One attempted bijection $X\to\mathbb{N}$ happens to fail.
$X$ is infinite, without comparing it with $\mathbb{N}$.
No bijection $X\to\mathbb{N}$ exists, even if $X$ is finite.

questions.question: If $A\subseteq X$ and $A$ is uncountable, what can you conclude about $X$?
options: $X$ is uncountable
$X$ is countably infinite
Nothing: $X$ may still be countable
$X\setminus A$ is uncountable

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a countable set from a countably infinite set?
options: A countable set may be finite; a countably infinite set is listable without end.
Every countable set is infinite and can be listed as $a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots$ without end.
A finite set is uncountable, since only infinite sets can be in bijection with $\mathbb{N}$.
A countably infinite listing eventually reaches a final element, as a finite listing does.

questions.question: How is a finite set classified under the countable/uncountable distinction?
options: Finite, so neither countable nor uncountable.
It is countable
It is uncountable
It is both countable and uncountable.

questions.question: Is the set $S=\{1/n \colon n\in\mathbb{N},\ n\ge 1\}$ countable?
options: Yes: $n\mapsto 1/n$ for $n\ge 1$ lists it.
No: its points pile up near $0$, as in an interval
No, because it is bounded.
Yes, because it is a finite subset of $[0,1]$
